```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, dev='png', out.width='100%')
report_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir=TRUE)))
project_root <- normalizePath(file.path(report_dir,'..','..','..'))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir=project_root)
```

```{r run-analysis, include=FALSE}
analysis <- new.env()
source(file.path(report_dir,'climate-spatial-residualisation.R'),local=analysis)
ss <- analysis$smooth_summary
main <- ss[ss$k==100,]
main <- main[order(match(main$variable,analysis$variables),main$atlas),]
fmt <- function(x, digits=3) formatC(x,format='f',digits=digits)
show_png <- function(suffix) knitr::include_graphics(file.path(report_dir,
  paste0('climate-spatial-residualisation-',suffix,'.png')),rel_path=FALSE)
climate_label <- function(variable) unname(analysis$variable_labels[variable])
summary_table <- function(d) data.frame(
  Climate=climate_label(d$variable),Atlas=d$atlas,
  `Original SD`=fmt(d$original_sd),`Residual SD`=fmt(d$residual_sd),
  `Variance retained (%)`=fmt(d$residual_variance_percent,1),
  EDF=fmt(d$edf,1),`Original Moran I`=fmt(d$original_moran),
  `Residual Moran I`=fmt(d$residual_moran),check.names=FALSE)
range_table <- data.frame(Climate=climate_label(main$variable),Atlas=main$atlas,
  `Original mean`=fmt(main$original_mean),
  `Original range`=paste(fmt(main$original_min),fmt(main$original_max),sep=' to '),
  `Residual range`=paste(fmt(main$residual_min),fmt(main$residual_max),sep=' to '),check.names=FALSE)
temp <- main[main$variable=='tmean_breeding',]
prec <- main[main$variable=='prec_breeding',]
sensitivity <- ss[order(match(ss$variable,analysis$variables),ss$atlas,ss$k),]
basis_table <- data.frame(Climate=climate_label(sensitivity$variable),Atlas=sensitivity$atlas,
  k=sensitivity$k,EDF=fmt(sensitivity$edf,1),
  `EDF / maximum (%)`=fmt(100*sensitivity$edf/sensitivity$basis_max_edf,1),
  `k-index`=fmt(sensitivity$k_index),
  Converged=sensitivity$gam_converged,check.names=FALSE)
```

<style>
table { display: block; max-width: 100%; overflow-x: auto; }
</style>

## Question and common data

How much temperature and precipitation variation remains after subtracting a
smooth geographical trend, and how spatially structured are the residuals?
This is an exploratory check of the climate information that could inform a
future Spatial+ analysis. It does not refit the bird models, estimate bird
responses, or demonstrate that spatial confounding has been resolved.

We use the **same 1,697 cells in all three atlases**, obtained by intersecting
the retained cells in the November forest-split preprocessing object. The full
fitted samples contained 1,747, 1,821, and 1,875 cells respectively. Climate and
coordinates are matched by cell identity, and coordinate equality is checked
across periods. No extra filtering or interpolation is applied.

Temperature is the March–June mean in **degrees Celsius**; precipitation is the
March–June total in **mm/season**, averaged over the atlas period by the upstream
preprocessing. Values are taken from the unstandardised environmental matrix
bundled with the November model inputs. These retain their original units;
residuals are not converted to z scores or rescaled to restore their original SD.

## Spatial decomposition

For each climate variable and atlas separately, we fit a Gaussian GAM:

\[
x_{i,a}=\alpha_a+f_a(E_i,N_i)+r_{i,a}.
\]

The fitted spatial trend is the intercept plus the two-dimensional thin-plate
smooth. The residual is the observed climate value minus that full fitted
trend. Easting and northing are centred and expressed in kilometres using the
stored EPSG:23032 coordinates. REML selects the smoothing parameter separately
for each fit.

This is a Euclidean spatial smooth, without coastline or water barriers. The
same specification includes the mainland, other islands, and Bornholm; the
map insets are a display choice rather than separate smoothing regions.

The main figures use basis dimension **k = 100**. We repeat the analysis with
**k = 50 and 200**. The basis dimension limits flexibility; it is not a fixed
spatial distance or the actual effective degrees of freedom (EDF). We report
EDF and basis diagnostics rather than selecting whichever fit removes the most
autocorrelation. See the [mgcv basis-dimension documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/choose.k.html).

The residual variance percentage is
\(100\,\operatorname{Var}(r)/\operatorname{Var}(x)\). It describes the variability
left in the detrended climate field. It is distinct from the percentage of SD
remaining, which is its square root after accounting for the percentage scale.
For example, retaining 25% of the original variance means retaining 50% of the
original SD.

## Main results: how much variation remains?

```{r main-summary}
knitr::kable(summary_table(main),caption='Main decomposition (k = 100): 1,697 cells in every fit. SDs retain the original climate units.')
```

After detrending with k = 100, temperature residuals retain
**`r fmt(min(temp$residual_variance_percent),1)`–`r fmt(max(temp$residual_variance_percent),1)`%**
of the original spatial variance, equivalent to
**`r fmt(min(temp$residual_sd_percent),1)`–`r fmt(max(temp$residual_sd_percent),1)`%**
of the original SD. Precipitation residuals retain
**`r fmt(min(prec$residual_variance_percent),1)`–`r fmt(max(prec$residual_variance_percent),1)`%**
of the original variance and
**`r fmt(min(prec$residual_sd_percent),1)`–`r fmt(max(prec$residual_sd_percent),1)`%**
of the original SD.

Thus substantial climate variation is represented by the smooth geographical
trends. There is still residual contrast among cells, but it covers a much
narrower range than the original climate gradients. The table below gives its
magnitude in physical units. Residuals can be negative: a negative value means
cooler or drier than the fitted local spatial trend, not negative absolute
temperature or rainfall.

```{r original-residual-ranges}
knitr::kable(range_table,caption='Original climate means/ranges and residual ranges at k = 100. Temperature in °C; precipitation in mm/season.')
```

## Temperature maps

Each row is an atlas; columns show original values, fitted spatial trend
including the intercept, and residuals. Original and fitted values share a
colour scale across all three atlases. Residuals have a separate common
zero-centred scale. All value ranges are included without clipping. Circular
points are cell locations, with Bornholm shown in each inset.

```{r temperature-maps}
show_png('tmean_breeding-maps')
```

## Precipitation maps

The same display rules apply, now in mm/season. Different residual and original
colour scales are necessary to see the residual patterns; compare their numeric
legends and SDs rather than interpreting colour intensity as equal magnitude.

```{r precipitation-maps}
show_png('prec_breeding-maps')
```

## Spatial autocorrelation before and after detrending

We use the same symmetrised four-nearest-neighbour graph for every field and
atlas: an edge is present if either cell selects the other among its four
nearest neighbours. Consequently, some cells have more than four neighbours.
Weights are row-standardised. The graph has **`r analysis$graph_components`
connected components**; disconnected geographical groups are retained.

Moran's I is reported as a descriptive measure of neighbouring similarity.
Ordinary independent-cell correlation p-values and Moran significance tests
are not calculated. Neighbourhood definition influences the statistic, so it
should be read alongside the distance-based diagnostics below.

At k = 100, residual Moran's I is
**`r fmt(min(temp$residual_moran))`–`r fmt(max(temp$residual_moran))`** for temperature
and **`r fmt(min(prec$residual_moran))`–`r fmt(max(prec$residual_moran))`** for
precipitation. Detrending reduces spatial autocorrelation but does **not**
eliminate it. These are residual climate fields, not independent observations.

### Temperature by distance

The upper row shows empirical semivariance in physical units. The middle row
divides each semivariogram by that field's own sample variance, making residual
spatial structure visible despite its reduced magnitude. The bottom row shows
unordered pair counts, identical across atlases and fields because we use the
same cells. Bins are (0,10], (10,20], …, (190,200] km. This 200-km limit applies
only to the displayed semivariograms; all cells inform the GAMs and the neighbour
graph.

```{r temperature-variograms}
show_png('tmean_breeding-variograms')
```

### Precipitation by distance

```{r precipitation-variograms}
show_png('prec_breeding-variograms')
```

The dashed value of one means semivariance equals the corresponding field's
sample variance. It is a reference, not proof of independence or a justified
cutoff for resampling. Open symbols flag bins with fewer than 100 pairs. No
confidence intervals or automatic spatial-range estimates are assigned.

```{r pair-counts}
knitr::kable(analysis$pair_counts,col.names=c('Bin','Midpoint (km)','Unordered pairs'),
  caption='Cell pairs contributing to each displayed distance bin; shared across all six climate fields.')
```

## Sensitivity to smoothing flexibility

```{r sensitivity-figure}
show_png('sensitivity')
```

Labels on the blue curves indicate k for the three settings used by every
atlas; horizontal positions indicate the smooth's actual EDF. Each
fit has its own REML-selected smoothing penalty. The sensitivity check asks how
the amount and spatial structure of residual climate depend on that adjustment.
It is not a competition to minimise Moran's I or residual variance. Finer
spatial adjustment can remove climate information needed for the intended
species-response question.

```{r sensitivity-summary}
tab <- summary_table(sensitivity)
tab <- cbind(tab[,1:2],k=sensitivity$k,tab[,-c(1,2)])
knitr::kable(tab,caption='Variation remaining and spatial autocorrelation for every basis setting.')
```

### Basis and convergence diagnostics

All 18 GAMs must pass the optimiser convergence checks before the report can
render. The k-index compares nearby residual differences with overall residual
variation. Low values can indicate remaining spatial structure or inadequate
basis flexibility; for these spatially correlated gridded climate fields they
are exploratory diagnostics, not an independent-error test proving that a
particular k is correct. EDF close to the basis maximum warrants particular
attention. No basis-diagnostic p-values are used to select a final adjustment.

For the main k = 100 fits, smooth EDF ranges from
**`r fmt(min(main$edf),1)` to `r fmt(max(main$edf),1)`**, out of a maximum of 99.
Together with the changes at k = 200, this underlines that the main display
is an exploratory adjustment, not a settled choice of spatial scale.

```{r basis-diagnostics}
knitr::kable(basis_table,caption='GAM convergence and basis diagnostics; no single adjustment is selected here.')
```

## Implications for changing species–climate responses

This check shows what climate contrasts remain after removing a specified smooth
spatial trend. It does not establish whether those remaining contrasts are
sufficient to estimate species responses: that depends on bird occurrence,
other predictors, sample support, and the outcome model.

In particular, each separate atlas fit subtracts its own intercept and smooth.
It removes the atlas's average climate level as well as broad spatial gradients.
The resulting residuals therefore do **not** retain all information about
warming, precipitation change, or broad-scale species–climate relationships.
A residual-based analysis asks about departures from the fitted geographical
trend. Extrapolating its coefficient to the original broad climate gradient
requires additional assumptions.

This is only a first-stage exploration motivated by
[Spatial+](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/biom.13656). It does not
replicate or validate a complete Spatial+ model for the multivariate Hmsc
analysis. Uncertainty in the fitted climate trend is not propagated here; no
first-stage or bird-model credible intervals are produced. Residual climate
is not guaranteed orthogonal to every possible spatial effect, and adjustment
of temperature and precipitation separately does not remove their mutual
correlation or confounding by other covariates.

A future outcome-model comparison would need to specify the spatial adjustment
consistently, inspect remaining climate support, propagate relevant uncertainty,
and test recovery of known constant and changing responses. We have not chosen
a final k, modified the environmental inputs, or refitted any bird models.

## Reproducibility and validation

Knit this document to rerun all 18 fits, regenerate the five PNGs, and embed them
in a self-contained HTML report. From the repository root:

```{r reproduction,echo=TRUE,eval=FALSE}
rmarkdown::render('scripts/5-vis/spatial-latents/climate-spatial-residualisation.Rmd')
```

The adjacent R script retains fitted GAMs, decomposition values, summaries,
common-cell IDs, spatial graph, semivariograms, and pair counts in memory. It
checks input alignment, identical coordinates across atlases, the 1,697-cell
intersection, finite values, optimiser convergence, approximately zero residual
means, and exact reconstruction of original climate as fitted trend plus
residual. Selected pair distances are independently checked against coordinate
differences; spatial weights and distance bins are reused across all fields.
All source inputs and fitted bird models are read only. Plots are PNG only.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
